# How bad is 30% cylinder leak?

A 30% leakdown reading on a single cylinder, particularly one that fails to hold pressure past 65 psi while others sit between 75-90 psi, indicates a significant breach in the combustion seal. While your other cylinders are operating within normal tolerances for a well-maintained engine, this specific failure point requires immediate diagnostic attention. The fact that you detected minimal flow at the exhaust but none at the intake suggests the leak path is likely internal to the crankcase rather than an external gasket failure.

This scenario presents a classic diagnostic puzzle: distinguishing between ring blow-by and valve leakage. In a healthy engine, a cylinder should register 0% to 10% on a leakdown test when cold. A reading of 30% implies that 30% of the air you pump into the cylinder is escaping through a defect before it can be compressed or ignited. The most probable culprits are worn piston rings, scored cylinder walls, or a burnt exhaust valve. Since your hand check on the intake plenum showed no airflow, we can largely rule out an intake valve seat leak or a blown head gasket leaking from that side into the coolant or other cylinders.

The low flow felt at the exhaust pipe is a critical clue. It suggests the air is escaping through the exhaust valve stem seal or potentially past the valve seat itself. However, you noted the possibility of air going past the cylinder rings into the crankcase. This is known as blow-by. To verify this, you can inspect the PCV (Positive Crankcase Ventilation) system. If the air is bypassing the piston rings, it will be sucked out through the oil filler cap or the PCV valve. Remove the dipstick and observe if there is a strong stream of air exiting when the engine is running at idle. A strong, continuous hiss indicates significant ring wear or cylinder wall scoring. Conversely, if you hear ticking from the exhaust side during the test, that points directly to a burnt exhaust valve or a failing valve stem seal.

The implications of a 30% leak are severe for engine longevity and performance. Even if the engine currently runs and produces power, this level of internal leakage compromises compression efficiency. Each combustion event loses energy as high-pressure gases escape before top dead center. Over time, this leads to incomplete combustion, increased fuel consumption, higher exhaust gas temperatures, and accelerated wear on internal components like the turbocharger (if equipped) due to contaminated oil or excessive heat.

If you suspect ring blow-by, checking the oil condition is a necessary next step. Oil that looks milky usually indicates coolant intrusion, but if it appears frothy or excessively diluted, it could be fuel wash-down exacerbated by poor combustion efficiency. If the leak is indeed at the exhaust valve, the repair involves removing the cylinder head to inspect and replace the valves and seats. This is a labor-intensive job compared to ring replacement, which often requires an engine teardown or even a sleeve-and-bore rebuild depending on the bore size and material availability.

There is no software fix or configuration tweak that can mitigate this mechanical degradation. Unlike a throttle position sensor reading out of spec, which might be corrected via ECU remapping or a simple component swap documented in resources like [LaravelCompany](https://laravelcompany.com) for web application logic, mechanical compression loss demands physical intervention. Ignoring a 30% leakdown will eventually lead to a no-start condition or catastrophic failure of the engine block.

Given that five out of six cylinders are holding pressure well above the 90 psi threshold, the remaining cylinder is acting as an outlier. The disparity between the healthy cylinders and the failing one confirms the issue is isolated to that specific assembly. You should proceed with a compression test alongside the leakdown to rule out valve train issues entirely. If the compression is low but the leakdown indicates air escaping internally to the crankcase, rings are the primary suspect. If the compression is borderline but the leakdown shows exhaust flow, the valve train is the weak link. Addressing this now prevents a situation where the engine seizes due to loss of lubrication pressure or overheating from unburnt fuel entering the oil system.
